canonical_statement: The study aimed to predict post-heparin activated partial thromboplastin time therapeutic state using machine-learning models to support optimization of heparin dosing in intensive care units.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The objective of this study was to predict the effects of heparin treatment using machine learning methods.

canonical_statement: The source databases initially contained 14,806 adult intensive-care-unit patients who received heparin therapy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Data were extracted from the databases for 14,806 adult patients who received heparin therapy.

population.label: Adult ICU patients receiving heparin therapy in MIMIC-III or eICU

canonical_statement: For the analytic cohort, patients were required to have an activated partial thromboplastin time measurement 4 to 6 hours after the initial heparin dose.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Only patient data with activated partial thromboplastin time measurements taken 4 to 6 hours after their initial heparin dose administration were used.

population.label: Heparin-treated adult ICU patients eligible for analysis
inclusion_criteria: aPTT measured 4 to 6 hours after the initial heparin dose

canonical_statement: Requiring a 4-to-6-hour post-dose activated partial thromboplastin time reduced the eligible cohort from 14,806 to 3,835 patients before later preprocessing exclusions.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Only patient data with activated partial thromboplastin time measurements taken 4 to 6 hours after their initial heparin dose administration were used which reduced the cohort size to 3835.

population.label: Heparin-treated adult ICU patients with 4-to-6-hour aPTT

canonical_statement: After outlier removal, the final modeled cohorts were MIMIC-III intravenous-push patients (data set 1, n=1,758), MIMIC-III intravenous-drip patients (data set 2, n=1,031), and eICU intravenous-drip patients (data set 3, n=575).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: After removing outliers, we extracted data on intravenous push patients (data set 1, n=1758) and intravenous drip patients (data set 2, n=1031).

population.label: Final modeled cohorts across MIMIC-III and eICU

canonical_statement: The analysis used the MIMIC-III and eICU research databases, which the authors described as free and open data sets.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The MIMIC-III database and eICU database are free and open data sets containing medical data.

canonical_statement: Subtherapeutic aPTT was defined as aPTT less than 60 seconds, using the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center therapeutic-range definition.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: subtherapeutic was defined as activated partial thromboplastin times less than 60 seconds

outcome.measurement_method: aPTT measured 4 to 6 hours after initial heparin dose

canonical_statement: Normal therapeutic aPTT was defined as aPTT from 60 to 100 seconds, using the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center therapeutic-range definition.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Normal therapeutic was defined as activated partial thromboplastin times from 60 seconds to 100 seconds

outcome.measurement_method: aPTT measured 4 to 6 hours after initial heparin dose

canonical_statement: Supratherapeutic aPTT was defined as aPTT greater than 100 seconds, using the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center therapeutic-range definition.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: supratherapeutic was defined as activated partial thromboplastin times greater than 100 seconds

outcome.measurement_method: aPTT measured 4 to 6 hours after initial heparin dose

canonical_statement: The candidate predictors were age, ethnicity, gender, initial heparin dose, time from initial heparin administration to first aPTT measurement, creatinine concentration, admission type, and AST/ALT ratio.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Clinical features of interest were selected to optimize the prediction of the therapeutic activated partial thromboplastin time—age, ethnicity, gender, initial heparin dose.

canonical_statement: Missing feature values were imputed with a k-nearest-neighbors algorithm based on Euclidean distance.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Missing values for some features were filled using the k–nearest neighbors algorithm.

canonical_statement: For continuous features, values with z scores outside -3 to +3 were removed before normalization; outliers were removed for heparin dose, creatinine, and AST/ALT ratio but not age.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: z scores outside of this range should be removed prior to normalization. Age data were found to be within the normal range; however, outliers were removed.

canonical_statement: The study compared support vector machine, random forest, adaptive boosting, extreme gradient boosting, and a shallow neural network for three-class aPTT-state prediction.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The support vector machine, random forest, adaptive boosting, extreme gradient boosting, and shallow neural network algorithms were implemented and tested.

canonical_statement: For model development, subtherapeutic, normal-therapeutic, and supratherapeutic samples were balanced at a 1:1:1 ratio; each data set was divided into 80% training/cross-validation and 20% testing.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Samples from subtherapeutic, normal therapeutic, and supratherapeutic data groups were included at a 1:1:1 ratio for training and validation. Each data set was divided into 80% training and cross-validation and 20% testing.

canonical_statement: The shallow neural network used two hidden layers with 36 and 24 neurons, ReLU activation, Adam optimization with initial learning rate 0.0015, 1,500 epochs, dropout rate 0.75, early stopping, and regularization.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: In the shallow neural network model, 2 hidden layers were used, and the number of neurons was set at 36/24 to reduce model complexity.

canonical_statement: Five-fold cross-validation was used to validate predictive performance, and grid search was used for support vector machine, random forest, adaptive boosting, and extreme gradient boosting hyperparameters.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The best parameters for the support vector machine, random forest, adaptive boosting, and extreme gradient boosting algorithms were searched (GridSearch).

canonical_statement: Model performance was evaluated with precision, recall, F1 score, and accuracy; the paper emphasized macroaveraged metrics for the balanced three-class task.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: we only compared the average accuracy and macroaveraged precision, recall, and F1 score to gauge the classification performances of these models.

canonical_statement: For the balanced experiments, 400 samples per class were selected for data set 1, 250 per class for data set 2, and 120 per class for data set 3; downsampling was used for subtherapeutic and normal classes and upsampling for the supratherapeutic class.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: we randomly selected 400 samples for each therapeutic state in data set 1, 250 samples for each therapeutic state in data set 2, and 120 samples for each therapeutic state in data set 3.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that the shallow neural network performed best among the tested models and recommended a parameter-adjustable shallow-neural-network support system for heparin treatment prediction.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: After comparing different models, we recommend the adoption of a support system comprising a shallow neural network with parameter adjustability.

canonical_statement: The authors interpreted comparable model performance across the three data sets as evidence that prediction was stable across administration routes and data sources.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The results suggested that model prediction performance was comparable among the 3 data sets, which gave us insight into the stability.

canonical_statement: The authors proposed that institutional differences in therapeutic aPTT ranges could be accommodated by adjusting shallow-neural-network parameters.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: our shallow neural network model can be adapted to different heparin administration guidelines by adjusting the parameters.

canonical_statement: The study did not balance or explicitly model the relative importance of discrete and continuous features.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: balancing both discrete features and continuous features and their relative importance would have enhanced model training performance and feature utilization but was not performed in this study.

canonical_statement: The authors noted that predictor features may be correlated and that intrinsic feature relationships were not determined.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: different features may have been correlated, since they all contribute to the comprehensive conditions of patients.

canonical_statement: The model had not been clinically deployed or prospectively validated; the authors stated that the nonclinical study would require further refinement in practice and validation on additional clinical data sets.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Since this study was conducted in a nonclinical setting, it will be further refined as it is used in practice.

canonical_statement: Drug interactions with heparin and accumulated effects were generally not included in the model.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Drug interactions with heparin and the accumulated effects are usually not taken into account.

canonical_statement: The article contains an internal metric-labeling inconsistency: the narrative labels class-specific shallow-neural-network values such as 79.35%, 93.15%, and 88.00% as F1 scores, while Tables 3-5 place those values in the precision column and report different F1 scores.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Considering the comprehensive performance which is best evaluated by F1 score, the shallow neural network achieved the best F1 score

canonical_statement: The article contains an internal sample-size inconsistency for data set 1: the Results text reports n=1,758, whereas Table 1 labels the MIMIC-III intravenous-push cohort as N=1,756.
